title: Rome grants living faith never without charity; Reformed grant fall from living love
source_text: XXXVII. Vicissim Scholae Romanae Doctores Reformatis concedunt, fidem vivam a charitate & bonis operibus separatam nunquam existere; nec ullam fidem actu servare & justificare, quae cum charitate & bonis operibus juncta non sit. Quod vero dicunt fidem quae jam per dilectionem operatur, & hominem in statu gratiae & salutis constituit, a dilectione separari posse, & in eo remanere in quo non amplius est ea charitas, & illud studium bonorum operum quae ad salutem necessaria sunt: quo casu fides ab actu justificandi cessat, nec pro illo tempore hominem Deo gratum reddit, & acceptum ad vitam aeternam, a Reformatis non negatur.
pass_a_gloss: Conversely Roman-school Doctors concede to the Reformed that living faith never exists separated from charity and good works; nor does any faith actually save and justify that is not joined with charity and good works. But what they say — that faith which already works through love and constitutes a man in the state of grace and salvation can be separated from love and remain in one in whom that charity and that pursuit of good works necessary for salvation are no longer: in which case faith ceases from the act of justifying, and for that time does not render the man pleasing to God and accepted to eternal life — is not denied by the Reformed.
pass_b_english: Rome grants: living faith never without charity; no actually-saving faith without works of love.
Reformed also grant: once-living faith can lose love, cease justifying for a time, and leave the person unaccepted.

lemmas.gloss: ceases from the act of justifying
